'''''Chamaecyparis formosensis''''' ('''Formosan cypress''', '''Taiwan cypress''', '''Taiwan red cypress''';<ref name="iucn status 17 November 2021" /> [[Chinese language|Chinese]]: 紅檜/红桧 ''hóngguì, Taiwan pron. hóngkuài'') is a species of large [[conifer]] in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]], [[endemism|endemic]] to [[Taiwan]], where it grows in the central mountains at moderate to high altitudes of 1000–2900 m. It is threatened by [[habitat loss]] and over-cutting for its valuable timber.<ref name="iucn status 17 November 2021" /><ref name=farjon>{{cite book |title=Monograph of Cupressaceae and ''Sciadopitys'' |last=Farjon |first=A. |year= 2005 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens |location=Kew |isbn=1-84246-068-4}}</ref><ref name=foc>Flora of China: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200005408 ''Chamaecyparis formosensis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080602092814/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200005408 |date=2008-06-02 }}</ref>

==Growth==
It is a slow-growing, but long-lived and ultimately large to very large [[Pinophyta|coniferous]] [[tree]] growing to 55–60 m tall with a trunk up to 7 m in diameter. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is red-brown, vertically fissured and with a stringy texture. The foliage is arranged in flat sprays; adult [[leaf|leaves]] are scale-like, 1–3 mm long, with pointed tips, green both above and below with only an inconspicuous [[stoma]]tal band at the base of each scale-leaf; they are arranged in opposite decussate pairs on the shoots. The juvenile leaves, found on young seedlings, are needle-like, 4–8 mm long, soft and glaucous bluish-green. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are ovoid-oblong, 6–12 mm long and 4–8 mm diameter, with 8–16 scales arranged in opposite pairs, maturing in autumn about 7–8 months after pollination.<ref name=farjon/>

==Related species==
It is most closely related to the Japanese ''[[Chamaecyparis pisifera]]'' (sawara cypress), which differs in smaller globose cones 4–8 mm long with 6–10 scales.<ref name=farjon/>

==Characteristics==
The [[wood]] is soft, very resistant to decay, and strongly scented; it is highly valued in traditional Taiwanese building, particularly for [[temple]]s and [[shrine]]s. This has led to excessive harvesting, resulting in the species now being endangered. A small number of the oldest and largest specimens are protected as national monuments, but much of the general population of the species still remains unprotected.<ref name=farjon/>

Essential oil distilled from its wood is uniquely scented and highly valued.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Su |first1=Sharleen |title=Distilling Taiwan's Native Scent |url=https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=032c2108-b881-4273-a6fe-5bc9289acc57&CatId=9 |website=www.taiwan-panorama.com |publisher=Taiwan Panorama |access-date=16 December 2020 |archive-date=27 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201127150126/https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=032c2108-b881-4273-a6fe-5bc9289acc57&CatId=9 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Notable examples ==
=== Sacred Tree of Alishan ===
The Sacred Tree of Alishan was a 3,000-year-old Taiwan red cypress which died from a lightning strike in 1956. The trunk remained standing until 1998. Due to its sacred status it was left alone by the Japanese when they deforested the surrounding area.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cheung |first1=Han |title=Taiwan inTime: Farewell to the divine giant |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2022/06/26/2003780571 |website=taipeitimes.com |date=26 June 2022 |publisher=Taipei Times |access-date=28 June 2022}}</ref>
